reasoning: The underlying problem — scoring frontier safety policies on how vague/aspirational vs. concrete/falsifiable their commitments are, and ranking labs comparatively from public documents — is substantially covered by existing published work. SaferAI's "Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks" (arXiv 2512.01166) applies a 65-criteria rubric to 12 frameworks, explicitly penalizing vague thresholds (e.g. "meaningful uplift") and discretionary language ("we may" vs "we will"), and produces a per-company leaderboard (Anthropic 34% to Cohere 8%) — essentially a vagueness/concreteness assessment with a ranking. METR's "Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies," the FLI AI Safety Index, AI Lab Watch, and arXiv 2508.08345 ("Do AI Companies Make Good on Voluntary Commitments...") all analyze commitment specificity/ambiguity across labs. The genuinely unexplored slice is the specific method: per-sentence segmentation of every commitment, a dedicated 1–5 falsifiable-vs-aspirational LLM-as-judge rubric over all sentences with Cohen's-kappa human validation, aggregated into a single reproducible "vagueness index." That automated, sentence-granular operationalization is a real (if incremental) gap, but the core contribution — which labs are vague and a comparative leaderboard — is already delivered by credible peer-style work, so gaps are minor.

evidence.title: Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks: Methodology and Results
evidence.summary: 65-criteria rubric scoring 12 frontier safety frameworks across four dimensions, producing a per-company leaderboard (34% Anthropic to 8% Cohere). Explicitly penalizes vague thresholds (e.g. 'meaningful uplift' undefined) and discretionary language ('we may' vs 'we will'), directly targeting the concrete-vs-vague distinction the proposal aims to measure.

evidence.title: Do AI Companies Make Good on Voluntary Commitments to the White House?
evidence.summary: Analyzes specificity and ambiguity of AI lab voluntary commitments, finding commitments are ambiguous, give generic high-level descriptions, and lack conditions for what constitutes satisfactory conduct. Recommends precise wording articulating goals and sufficient evidence of completion.

evidence.title: Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies (December 2025 Update)
evidence.summary: Comparative analysis across labs of capability thresholds, halting conditions, and mitigations, noting most companies lack clearly defined binding commitments to halt development when thresholds approach — the vagueness problem the proposal addresses.

evidence.title: AI Safety Index: Summer/Winter 2025
evidence.summary: Scored, graded leaderboard of major AI labs' safety practices including governance and commitment quality — an existing per-lab safety ranking covering similar comparative-scoring ground.

evidence.title: I read every major AI lab's safety plan so you don't have to
evidence.summary: Comparative qualitative reading and assessment of every major lab's safety plan, identifying which commitments are concrete actions vs aspirations — community precedent for the comparative vagueness assessment, though manual rather than LLM-judged.

evidence.title: Methodology – Risk Management Ratings
evidence.summary: Public methodology for a reproducible 0-100% per-criterion grading of lab frameworks with a uniform grading scale and finer gradations at extremes; a maintained ratings leaderboard closely analogous to the proposed vagueness leaderboard.
